subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Bargaining and Fairness Norms
description: A quick win: understand Bargaining and Fairness Norms.

hook.text: Union and management sit in a room. Both have a zone of agreement. But anchoring, fairness norms, and ego keep them.

buildup.text: Bargaining theory predicts quick efficient outcomes. Real negotiations stall because both sides use different fairness.

discovery.text: Babcock found self-serving bias in fairness: each side selects evidence supporting their preferred outcome.

twist.text: Strikes and lawsuits often cost more than the disputed amount. The fight is about principle, not profit.

climax.text: In negotiations, understand the other side's fairness frame. Resolving the frame conflict often resolves.

punchline.text: Negotiations stall on principle, not on dollars.

quiz.question: What is self-serving bias in negotiations?
options: Each side genuinely believing their preferred outcome is the fair one
Always accepting the other party's first offer

details.summary: Real bargaining behavior deviates from rational predictions because people care about fairness, not just outcomes. Bargainers reject profitable deals they perceive as unfair and accept worse deals that feel equitable.
details.whyItMatters: Fairness norms shape negotiations in labor markets, international trade, and everyday transactions. Ignoring them leads to failed deals and broken relationships, even when the economics suggest both sides should agree.
takeaways: People reject profitable offers they perceive as unfair
Fairness norms vary across cultures but exist universally
Equal splits are the most common outcome in bargaining experiments

faq.question: Why do people reject offers that would make them better off?
faq.answer: Rejecting an unfair offer punishes the proposer and enforces fairness norms, even at personal cost. This willingness to sacrifice gains to punish unfairness helps maintain cooperative social norms in the long run.

faq.question: Do fairness norms differ across cultures?
faq.answer: Yes significantly. Experiments across 15 small-scale societies found wide variation in what constitutes a fair split. Some cultures offer hyperfair amounts, others offer minimal shares. Market integration correlates with higher fairness offers.
